opus-5.5.text:
Data has been the main driver of progress so far. If you look at the past several years, most of the big jumps came from scaling: more data, more compute, bigger models. The scaling laws tell us that if you keep feeding the model more high-quality tokens, the loss keeps going down in a fairly predictable way. So in that sense, data is the fuel.

But I think we're reaching a point where we have to ask a more fundamental question. A human child doesn't read trillions of tokens. A person might see a few hundred million words in a lifetime, yet we generalize, reason, and pick up new concepts from just a handful of examples. Current models need orders of magnitude more data to get comparable abilities. That gap tells us something is missing. It's not only about the amount of data. It's about how the model learns from it.

So I see the role of data shifting in a few ways.

First, quality and structure matter more than raw quantity. We've already seen that carefully curated or synthetic data, like reasoning traces, math proofs, and code with verification, can be much more valuable per token than random web text. Data that exposes the underlying structure of a problem helps the model learn the right representation rather than just memorizing surface patterns.

Second, there's the question of where new data comes from once we've used up most of the high-quality human text. One answer is self-generated data: the model explores, tries solutions, gets feedback from a verifier or an environment, and learns from that. That's essentially what reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks does. The model is producing its own training signal, a bit like how humans learn by practicing and making mistakes, not just by reading.

Third, and this is the part I personally find most interesting, we need to understand the learning mechanism itself. In my research I spend a lot of time trying to open up the black box: how does a Transformer actually pick up features from data, why does attention become sparse, how do representations emerge during training? If we understand those dynamics, we might find that much of the data we use is redundant, and that with the right inductive bias or training objective, a model could learn the same thing from far fewer examples. That's how you approach human-like efficiency, not by brute force, but through insight.

So my view is that data got us here, but data alone probably won't get us to human-level efficiency. The next step is combining better data, interaction and feedback, and a much deeper theoretical understanding of how these models learn. When those come together, I think we'll see models that need far less data and generalize much better, and that's when AI starts to look more like how humans actually think.

r004.rationale: It says human-like efficiency may come from a better inductive bias or training objective, enabling models to learn the same things from fewer examples.

r005.rationale: It states that scaling with more high-quality tokens lowers loss predictably and that more data helped drive recent progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think data is really the central question right now, and the honest answer is that we've been using it very inefficiently.

Look at how current models learn. We throw trillions of tokens at them, and they get strong, but the amount of data they consume is orders of magnitude beyond what any human sees in a lifetime. A child learns language from maybe tens of millions of words. A model needs something like a hundred thousand times more. So the gap isn't really about scale anymore. It's about how much a system extracts from each example.

My view is that there are two things going on. First, data quality matters far more than data quantity once you pass a certain point. The web is full of redundancy, and a lot of the recent gains have come from curation, synthetic data, and filtering rather than just scraping more. That's a sign that the bottleneck is shifting from "how much can we collect" to "what is actually informative."

Second, and this is what I find more interesting, humans don't just absorb data passively. We have strong inductive biases, we form hypotheses, and we actively seek out the experiences that resolve our uncertainty. A lot of human sample efficiency comes from structure that's already there, from reasoning, from being able to compose a few primitives into many situations. Current models mostly learn by pattern matching over enormous corpora, and when you look inside them you often see they've memorized shortcuts instead of discovering the underlying rule.

So if the goal is human-like efficiency, I don't think the path is simply better data. I think it's models that can do more with each piece of data, through reasoning, through search, through learning from their own interaction with an environment rather than only from static text. Reinforcement learning and self-play are early examples of this. The system generates its own experience and the signal comes from outcomes, not from a human writing down the answer.

That said, I'd be careful about the framing. Humans are efficient in some ways and extremely inefficient in others. We take twenty years to become useful. The real target is probably not copying human learning, but understanding why certain structures let you generalize from very little, and building that into the architecture and the training process. Data will always matter, but the leverage is in how the model uses it.

astra-6.text:
I think data is central, but the question is not simply how much data we have. It’s what the model can learn from each experience. Two datasets of the same size can have very different value depending on their quality, diversity, and how they’re presented during training.

Humans are remarkably efficient in that sense. We can see a few examples, connect them to what we already know, and apply that understanding to a new situation. But we also bring a lot of prior experience. A child learning a new word isn’t starting from scratch—they already have experience with objects, people, and the physical world. So comparing the number of examples alone can be misleading.

For AI, I think an important direction is to move beyond passively consuming data. A model should be able to interact, make a prediction, try something, and learn from the outcome. Then the question becomes: which experience would help it learn the most? That connects data with exploration and reasoning.

So more data can certainly make models stronger, but human-like efficiency will also require better ways to use it: building reusable knowledge, transferring it across tasks, and seeking out information when something is missing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data is central, but the question is not simply how much data we can collect. It is also what information the data contains and how efficiently a model can learn from it. If you give a model many examples that are essentially the same, you may get much less benefit than from a smaller set that exposes something new.

Humans seem to learn with much less explicit training, although the comparison is complicated. We have prior knowledge, we interact with the world, and we choose what to pay attention to. We don’t just passively read a fixed dataset. We try something, observe the result, and update our understanding.

So I think moving toward human-like efficiency requires improving both the data and the learning process. A model should be able to identify what it doesn’t understand, seek useful experience, and use feedback to improve. More data can make models stronger, but learning more from each experience is the deeper challenge.
